title: These Planets Are Fluffier Than Cotton Candy!
summary: Imagine a planet as big as Jupiter — but so light it could float in water like a beach ball! That's exactly what scientists just found. Two new planets, called superpuffs, are the fluffiest worlds ever seen. They're each about the size of Jupiter, but their mass is tiny. One has the mass of 9.5 Earths, the other 18.6 Earths. Compare that to Jupiter, which is 317 times Earth's mass! In fact, their density is around 0.04 grams per cubic centimeter. That's about the same as cotton candy or shaving foam. These superpuffs orbit a star named TOI 791, which is 1,113 light-years from Earth. A space telescope called TESS spotted them when they passed in front of their star and blocked a little bit of its light. But to find their density, scientists needed their mass too. That's where a special telescope in Antarctica helped. Because the planets take 12 hours to cross their star, only Antarctica had long enough nights to watch the whole thing. By tracking how the planets tug on each other's orbits, researchers figured out their masses. How do such light planets form? One idea is they started far from their star and moved closer, puffing up as they heated up. Or maybe they're still young and cooling down. Next, the James Webb Space Telescope will study their atmospheres. Finding these rare worlds helps us understand how planets — even Earth — fit into the big picture of the universe.
why_it_matters: Looking at wacky planets like these teaches us about all the ways a planet can be made, which helps us figure out how our own Earth came to be and if there are other worlds like it.

background_read: Astronomers have found over 5,000 planets outside our solar system, and some of them are very strange, like these superpuffs that are huge but weigh almost nothing.
TESS (a NASA telescope that searches for planets) spots worlds by noticing tiny dips in starlight when a planet crosses in front of its star, just like a little eclipse.
The James Webb Space Telescope, which launched in 2021 and is the most powerful space telescope ever, can look at the gases around distant planets to learn what they are made of.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists and researchers studying planets outside our solar system.
WHAT: The discovery of two superpuff planets – worlds as large as Jupiter but with the density of cotton candy.
WHERE: They orbit a star called TOI 791, 1,113 light-years away from Earth.
WHY: Studying such unusual planets helps astronomers understand how different worlds form and how Earth fits into the big picture of the universe.

perspectives.description: Finding cotton-candy planets is amazing because space is full of surprises, and it shows that not every world is rocky like Earth or gassy like Jupiter.
These superpuffs give us important clues about how solar systems are born. By studying them, we can test our ideas and maybe discover rules we never knew existed.
Some people think we should spend money on problems here on Earth instead of looking at faraway planets, but space discoveries often lead to new technology that helps everyone.
